source.title: Multilingual Language Models Encode Script Over Linguistic Structure
source.citation: Aastha A. K. Verma et al., 2026
source.authors: Aastha A. K. Verma; Anwoy Chatterjee; Mehak Gupta; Tanmoy Chakraborty

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present. Some plotted values are not given numerically in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses different measurements and interventions to investigate what language-associated units encode. Its results concern script sensitivity and linguistic structure, but do not directly measure the unrelated-input polysemanticity specified in the listed versions.
record.gate_note: The paper measures language-associated units identified by LAPE or SAE-LAPE under script and word-order perturbations, probes typological information, and intervenes on selected units. These results bear on unit interpretation but do not measure polysemantic responses to unrelated tokens or contexts as specified by V1–V7. Related work cited in the paper is not recorded as a result.
record.test_reason: The study identifies language-associated MLP neurons and SAE features with LAPE/SAE-LAPE. It measures how their overlap changes under romanization and word shuffling, probes them for typology, and ablates them. It never measures how many neurons respond to unrelated inputs, what causes that, or how it varies with architecture or measurement. Polysemanticity appears only as a background assumption: raw neurons are called 'typically denser and more polysemantic' to justify a stricter filter, and SAEs are motivated as separating overlapping signals. No result bears on V1–V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that language-associated units are organized mainly around surface form, especially script. Romanized inputs form near-disjoint unit sets aligned with neither native script nor English, and this persists at 8B/9B despite translation competence. Typological information becomes more accessible with depth. Generation depends most on units invariant to surface perturbations. Overall, multilingual LMs do not form a unified interlingua.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses LAPE/SAE-LAPE, script romanization and word shuffling, typological probes, and targeted ablations; it does not reproduce the original vision-neuron analysis or SoLU comparison.
record.method_sensitivity: Unit overlap and typological alignment differ by representation (raw neurons versus SAE features), perturbation (script versus word-order shuffling), language, and model. The paper reports selective SAE instability under shuffling and model-dependent probing patterns.

fits_no_version.finding: Language-associated units identified from native and romanized inputs overlap little (Jaccard typically <0.3), and overlap with English is near zero. The pattern persists at 8B/9B scale.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Language-associated units in multilingual LMs are conditioned on script rather than on abstract language identity.

fits_no_version.finding: Word-order shuffling largely preserves language-associated unit sets. SAE features show selective instability for some Latin-script languages.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Language-associated units are more stable under word-order perturbation than under script change.

fits_no_version.finding: Units shared across native and romanized inputs show the strongest typological probing alignment.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Script-invariant language-associated units carry more linearly accessible typological information.

fits_no_version.finding: Zero-ablating shuffling-invariant overlap neurons degrades perplexity more than random controls and causes within-word script mixing. Mean-replacing only-native neurons causes language switching.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Language-associated neuron groups defined by invariance have distinct causal roles in generation.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The paper analyzes MLP activations and SAE features, not attention heads or embeddings. The detailed core causal experiments use the first 100 FLORES+ examples per language; the reported evidence does not address training dynamics or models larger than 9B. Many per-language overlap and probing values appear in plots without exact numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: The record omits supplementary activation-entropy and activation-probability distributions, detailed per-language plot values not stated numerically in the text, and qualitative generation examples; these do not measure any listed version.

untested.parts: Vision classifiers; no image models studied.
Share of MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts, and its variation by layer. Only language-selective neurons are studied.
Superposition as the cause of polysemanticity. SAEs are used as a tool only.
Effect of activation function, architecture or regularization on the share of polysemantic neurons, and its performance cost.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons reflect one shared feature.
Dependence of the polysemantic classification on activation range or scoring method.

record.verdict_notes: This is an ACL multilingual-interpretability paper. Its only contact with the polysemanticity claim is an assumption that raw neurons are 'more polysemantic', used to set a percentile filter, plus SAE motivation. It does not cite Zoom In or SoLU. The reader's 'tests/T2' is wrong given that all rows are versions=['none'] and every version is untested. The states on rows are judged against the study's own hypotheses, not against any claim version.

versions.untested_parts: Vision classifiers and the InceptionV1 neuron example.
The share of MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts, and variation in that share across layers.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by superposition or capacity pressure.
Polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization, or training noise when capacity is sufficient.
The share of polysemantic neurons across activation functions, architectures, or regularization settings, and the effect on performance.
Whether apparent unrelated mixtures in canonical polysemantic neurons share a coherent feature or job.
Whether polysemanticity classification changes with activation range or explanation-scoring method.
